Readers of every tradition largely agree on this verse.

## The reading within Judaism
The psalm is David’s, and the shepherd is the God of Israel, who led his people out of Egypt like a flock and feeds them still; the second line is the trust of one who has been kept. The weight falls on the one word shepherd, and on the psalm as Israel’s own prayer. Held by Jewish readers of every tradition.

## The Christian reading
Christians pray the same trust and hear the shepherd again in the Gospel, where Jesus calls himself the good shepherd, so the verse is prayed as his. The weight falls on the word shepherd and on the Gospel’s use of it. Held by the churches alike.

## Where they agree
Both read the shepherd as God’s own care, and the second line as trust in it.

## Where they part, and why
- Whether the shepherd is heard again in the Gospel: a question of what else is read with the psalm.

## Where readings can be held together
A description of care can carry a personal meaning and a communal meaning together if neither excludes the other. These possible applications require a broader interpretive context; compatibility alone establishes neither.

## What the text settles
The shepherd is the LORD, and the one who speaks wants for nothing; the verse names no occasion and no enemy.

## Questions to take back to the text
1. Read the whole psalm: where does the shepherd give way to the host?
2. What does the second line promise, and what does it leave out?
3. What did you bring to the word shepherd before you read the verse?
